blocks.text: The path of a hormone's message

An endocrine gland secretes its hormone in response to a particular stimulus. The blood carries the hormone to all cells, but only target cells, which have receptors that bind that specific hormone, respond. Binding triggers events that change the cell. Receptors may be on the cell membrane, in the cytoplasm or in the nucleus.

blocks.title: Hormones and neurotransmitters
blocks.text: Both are chemical messengers, but hormones belong to the endocrine system and neurotransmitters to the nervous system. Hormones are usually slower to act and have longer-lasting effects.

blocks.prompt: Where are the receptors for insulin and for testosterone, and why?
blocks.explanation: Insulin, a water-soluble protein, cannot cross the membrane, so its receptors are on the cell surface. Testosterone, a lipid-soluble steroid, crosses the membrane, so its receptors are inside the cell.

items: Protein/peptide and glycoprotein hormones: surface receptors. Amino acid derivatives: some cross (T3, T4), some do not (epinephrine). Steroids (from cholesterol): cross, act on the nucleus.
